screens.title: Layer 2 Security Features and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Layer 2 is where most devices first meet the network, and many powerful attacks start there. In this lesson you will learn the essential Layer 2 controls available on Catalyst switches: Port Security to limit MAC learning, DHCP Snooping to prevent rogue servers and starvation, Dynamic ARP Inspection to stop ARP spoofing, IP Source Guard to block IP/MAC spoofing, and Storm Control to contain traffic floods. You will see how these features work together — DHCP Snooping builds a binding table that DAI and IP Source Guard rely on — and where common operational mistakes occur, such as enabling DAI before DHCP Snooping or using shutdown violation actions without errdisable recovery. We will use configuration excerpts and verification commands to show how these controls prevent real attacks like MAC flooding, DHCP starvation, and ARP poisoning. By the end you will understand the practical trade-offs of each feature, a checklist for safe rollout, and a short hands-on scenario to practice configuring and verifying Layer 2 defenses. Think about how access port behavior and trusted/untrusted classification influences the protections you can apply.

keyIdea.title: Why Layer 2 matters
keyIdea.text: Access-layer controls stop many serious attacks before they reach routers or firewalls. Layer 2 features must be deployed in a coordinated way, since some protections depend on others.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Layer 2 Security Features
Layer 2 Security Features and Best Practices
Core defenses for access switching: limit, verify, validate, and contain link-layer threats.
In this lesson
You will learn Port Security, DHCP Snooping, DAI, IP Source Guard, Storm Control, and safe operational patterns for production switches.
Why it matters
Layer 2 attacks can give an attacker network-wide visibility or disrupt services. Properly configured access switches prevent many common breaches.
Explore Key Topics
Port Security
Restrict MAC learning, sticky addresses, and violation modes.
DHCP Snooping & DAI
Builds a binding table used to validate DHCP and ARP traffic.
IPSG & Storm Control
Filter spoofed sources and limit broadcast storms.
Visual Overview
Feature cards and relationships
Port Security
Limits MACs learned and sets violation actions: protect, restrict, shutdown.
DHCP Snooping → DAI → IPSG
DHCP Snooping builds the binding table. DAI and IPSG validate packets against that table.
Storm Control
Drops excessive broadcasts, multicasts or unknown unicasts when thresholds are exceeded.
Starter Scenario
AccessSW1 with Gi1/0/1 user access and Gi1/0/24 trusted uplink on VLAN 10. We'll step through configuration and verification of features that protect Gi1/0/1.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this module you will acquire practical skills to secure the access layer. First, you will identify common Layer 2 attack vectors such as MAC address flooding, DHCP starvation, ARP spoofing, and VLAN hopping. Knowing the attack patterns helps you choose the right control and set thresholds conservatively. Second, you will configure Port Security to limit MAC addresses per port, choose sticky or static bindings, and understand the impact of violation modes. You will practice using protect, restrict, and shutdown and learn when to enable errdisable recovery to minimize outages. Third, you will implement DHCP Snooping — mark trusted and untrusted ports, enable snooping per VLAN, and inspect the binding table to spot anomalies. Fourth, you will enable Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard to validate ARP and IP/MAC bindings based on the DHCP Snooping table, and configure Storm Control to defend against traffic storms. Each objective includes verification steps so you can confirm protections are active and effective in a production-like environment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Verification & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Learning to configure controls is only half the task — you must also verify they work and troubleshoot when they don't. In this objective set you'll practice verification commands and interpret their output. For Port Security you will use show commands to list secure MAC addresses, violation counters, and errdisabled state. For DHCP Snooping you'll inspect the binding table to confirm leases and detect suspicious entries. For DAI you'll review arp inspection counters and verify trusted interfaces. For IP Source Guard you'll confirm that source verification is active and that traffic is being filtered for mismatched IP/MAC pairs. Finally, for Storm Control you'll check interface counters and threshold events to confirm the switch is dropping excess broadcast or multicast traffic. Each verification objective includes a common-mistake check: for example, DHCP Offers dropped by an untrusted uplink, or DAI failing because DHCP Snooping was not enabled. These checks help you move from configuration to operational certainty.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Verification Objectives
Port Security Checks
  • Show secure MACs and violation counters for a specific interface.
  • Confirm errdisable recovery interval if using shutdown violation mode.
  • Identify sticky MACs saved to running-config after reboots.
DHCP Snooping & DAI Checks

screens.title: Port Security Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Port Security restricts how many MAC addresses a switch port will learn and which MAC addresses are allowed. Its purpose is to reduce the risk from MAC address table flooding attacks and to prevent unauthorized devices from sharing a legitimate endpoint's link. There are three common learning modes: dynamic learning, where the switch learns MACs as devices send traffic; static configuration, where you enter exact MAC addresses you trust; and sticky learning, where the switch learns MACs dynamically but remembers those learned addresses in the running configuration. Violation modes determine the operational response when an unauthorized MAC is seen: protect drops the frames without logging, restrict drops frames and increments a counter and logs events, and shutdown error-disables the interface until manually recovered or errdisable recovery re-enables it. A concrete example is configuring Gi1/0/1 to allow two sticky MACs for a PC and an IP phone. A common mistake is selecting shutdown without errdisable recovery, which can keep a port down for legitimate users after an accidental violation. When you apply Port Security, always monitor violation counters and choose the least disruptive mode that still enforces policy. How would you balance security and availability on a desk with a user and phone?

keyIdea.title: Port Security claim
keyIdea.text: Limit MAC learning per port and choose learning and violation modes to balance protection and availability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Port Security Fundamentals
Definition
Port Security restricts MAC address learning and enforces violation actions.
  • Learning modes: dynamic, static, sticky.
  • Violation actions: protect, restrict, shutdown (error-disable).
  • Monitoring: violation counters, show port-security output.
Concrete example
Allow two sticky MACs on Gi1/0/1 so a workstation and a phone can share the access port; choose restrict for logging instead of shutdown during rollout.
Key Takeaway

Start with sticky learning and restrict mode for production; move to stricter actions after validation.

Configuration snippet
configure terminal interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 switchport mode access switchport access vlan 10 switchport port-security switchport port-security maximum 2 switchport port-security mac-address sticky switchport port-security violation restrict
Common mistake
Using shutdown without errdisable recovery can keep legitimate users offline after an accidental violation. Prefer restrict or ensure automatic recovery is configured during testing.

screens.title: Port Security Violation Modes Compared
screens.narratorSegment: When a port observes an unauthorized MAC, the switch can respond in three ways: protect, restrict, or shutdown. Protect silently drops frames from unknown MACs and allows normal traffic from known MACs to continue. It is the least disruptive but offers no notifications. Restrict also drops frames, but it increments violation counters and generates logs or SNMP traps, giving visibility while avoiding immediate outage. Shutdown is the strictest: the interface is error-disabled until manually recovered or errdisable recovery re-enables it after a configured interval. This is highly secure because it physically removes the port from forwarding, but it can cause long outages for legitimate users if misapplied. Consider a port that serves both an IP phone and a laptop. If you expect MAC churn, protect or restrict is safer during an initial rollout. If the port is dedicated to a single device in a secure closet, shutdown with errdisable recovery set may be appropriate. Always document expected device counts and test behavior under realistic conditions. A common misconception is that shutdown is always better; in fact, without automated recovery it increases operational risk. Which mode you pick should match your availability requirements, logging needs, and incident response process.

keyIdea.title: Violation trade-off
keyIdea.text: Protect for minimal disruption, restrict for visibility, shutdown for strict enforcement — choose based on availability requirements and recovery automation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Violation Modes
Protect
Drops unknown MAC frames silently
Minimal disruption, no logs. Use when you want to avoid outages and accept less visibility.
Restrict
Drops frames and logs violations
Balanced: gives alerts and counters without immediately disabling the port.
Shutdown
Error-disables the interface
Most secure but disruptive. Pair with errdisable recovery if used in production to avoid long outages.
Operational guidance
  • Start with restrict to gather visibility, then consider stricter actions once you understand normal behavior.
  • Document expected devices and MAC counts per port before tightening limits.
  • Enable errdisable recovery when using shutdown in environments where human response may be delayed.

screens.title: DHCP Snooping Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: DHCP Snooping defends the network from rogue DHCP servers that can hand out incorrect addresses and from DHCP starvation attacks that exhaust the server's pool. It works by classifying interfaces as trusted or untrusted. Trusted ports are connected to legitimate DHCP servers or upstream switches and are allowed to send all DHCP messages, including server-originated messages like Offer and ACK. Untrusted ports, typically access ports, are restricted and will only forward client-originated messages; server messages from untrusted ports are dropped. DHCP Snooping also builds a binding table mapping client MAC addresses, leased IP addresses, VLANs, and the interface on which the lease was observed. This table becomes a critical source of truth for other features such as Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard. A concrete example is enabling DHCP Snooping globally and for VLAN 10 and marking the uplink port to the distribution switch as trusted. A common misconception is that DHCP Snooping is an isolated feature — in practice it is foundational: enabling DAI or IPSG without a healthy DHCP Snooping binding table will cause false positives. During rollout, monitor the binding table and logs for dropped server messages to ensure trusted uplinks are configured correctly.

keyIdea.title: DHCP Snooping claim
keyIdea.text: Classify ports as trusted or untrusted, collect bindings, and prevent rogue DHCP responses; this binding table is used by other protections.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › DHCP Snooping
Definition
Validate DHCP exchanges and build a binding table.
  • Trusted vs untrusted ports control which DHCP messages are allowed.
  • Binding table stores MAC, IP, VLAN, and interface — the source of truth for other features.
  • Prevents rogue DHCP servers and DHCP starvation attacks.
Concrete example
Enable snooping globally, enable VLAN 10, and mark the uplink Gi1/0/24 as trusted so DHCP Offers from the server are forwarded.
Watchpoint

If an uplink is left untrusted, legitimate DHCP Offer and ACK packets will be dropped and clients will fail to obtain addresses.

Configuration snippet
ip dhcp snooping ip dhcp snooping vlan 10 ip dhcp snooping database flash:dhcp_snooping.db interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24 ip dhcp snooping trust
After enabling, use show ip dhcp snooping binding to confirm leases and show ip dhcp snooping statistics to review dropped messages.

screens.title: DHCP Snooping Binding Table and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: The DHCP Snooping binding table is the key artifact produced by DHCP Snooping. It maps client MAC addresses to IP addresses, VLANs, lease times, and the switch interface where the lease was observed. You will use the binding table to identify legitimate leases and spot anomalies such as many leases from the same MAC (possible spoofing) or leases on unexpected interfaces. To verify, run show ip dhcp snooping binding and examine entries for VLAN, MAC, IP, and interface. If you suspect DHCP starvation, watch the binding table for rapid churn or many incomplete bindings. Another verification step is to check which ports are trusted with show ip dhcp snooping interfaces and ensure uplinks to DHCP servers are trusted. Example output shows a binding for 00:11:22:33:44:55 with IP 10.0.10.25 on Gi1/0/1. A common mistake is relying on stale or missing bindings if the snooping database or forwarding path to the database is misconfigured. Always confirm the snooping database is enabled if persistent storage is required, and monitor logs for dropped server messages after toggling trust settings. How would you respond if you saw DHCP Offers dropped from an uplink?

keyIdea.title: Binding table use
keyIdea.text: Use the binding table to validate IP-MAC-interface associations and detect suspicious lease behavior before enabling dependent features.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › DHCP Binding Table
What to inspect
  • MAC, IP, VLAN, interface, lease time.
  • Look for multiple IPs per MAC or leases appearing on the wrong interface.
  • Check bindings rapidly increasing during a suspected starvation attack.
Verification commands
Use show ip dhcp snooping binding and show ip dhcp snooping statistics; confirm trusted interfaces with show ip dhcp snooping interface.
Key Takeaway

Confirm bindings and trusted uplinks before enabling DAI or IPSG to avoid false positives.

Example output
Switch# show ip dhcp snooping binding MacAddress IpAddress Lease(sec) Type VLAN Interface 00:11:22:33:44:55 10.0.10.25 86397 dhcp 10 Gi1/0/1 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff 10.0.10.26 86399 dhcp 10 Gi1/0/2 Switch# show ip dhcp snooping statistics Packets dropped: DHCP Offer: 0, DHCP Ack: 0
If Offers are dropped on a legitimate uplink, ensure that the uplink interface is configured with ip dhcp snooping trust.

screens.title: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic ARP Inspection stops ARP spoofing by validating ARP packets against a trusted source of bindings — the DHCP Snooping table. When enabled for a VLAN, DAI inspects ARP requests and replies received on untrusted ports and checks whether the source IP-to-MAC mapping matches an entry in the binding table. If it does not match, the ARP packet is dropped. DAI also validates ARP header fields to prevent malformed ARP frames. Because of this dependency, DHCP Snooping must be enabled and correctly populating bindings before DAI is activated; otherwise legitimate ARP traffic can be mistakenly discarded. A practical example: enable ip arp inspection vlan 10 and mark the uplink as trusted so legitimate ARP replies from the gateway are allowed. A common misconception is that DAI works independently of DHCP Snooping — in reality, absent valid bindings you will see increased drops. When enabling DAI, plan a staged rollout: enable DHCP Snooping, confirm bindings, then enable DAI with monitoring mode or on a small set of interfaces first. This reduces the risk of causing a widespread ARP failure for users.

keyIdea.title: DAI dependency
keyIdea.text: DAI enforces ARP validation using DHCP Snooping bindings; enable and verify snooping before enabling DAI to avoid false positives.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Dynamic ARP Inspection
Definition
Inspect ARP packets and validate IP-to-MAC bindings.
  • Checks ARP packets on untrusted ports against DHCP Snooping bindings.
  • Drops mismatched ARP to prevent ARP poisoning and interception.
  • Requires trusted uplinks for legitimate server/gateway ARP traffic.
Configuration hint
Enable DHCP Snooping first. Then use ip arp inspection vlan 10 and mark uplinks with ip arp inspection trust. Monitor arp inspection counters for dropped packets after enabling.
Analogy
Think of DHCP Snooping as a guest list and DAI as the security guard checking IDs against that list before letting ARP announcements through.

screens.title: DAI Troubleshooting and Safe Rollout
screens.narratorSegment: When enabling Dynamic ARP Inspection, follow a staged process so you avoid unintentionally blocking legitimate traffic. Start by enabling DHCP Snooping and verify the binding table contains expected entries for critical hosts, such as the default gateway and servers. Next, enable DAI on a single VLAN and configure uplink interfaces as trusted. After enabling DAI, monitor show ip arp inspection statistics and show ip dhcp snooping binding to correlate dropped ARP with missing bindings. If you see legitimate ARP being dropped, the likely causes are: DHCP Snooping not enabled on that VLAN, the uplink not configured as trusted, or stale/missing entries in the binding table for statically configured hosts. To handle statically assigned addresses, you can configure static entries in the ARP inspection table or add manual static entries to the binding table where supported. During troubleshooting, consider temporarily placing DAI in a monitoring posture by tracking counters without tight enforcement, or apply DAI to a subset of interfaces first. A misconception is that DAI is an all-or-nothing switch — careful, phased application reduces risk and gives you time to address exceptions.

keyIdea.title: Safe DAI rollout
keyIdea.text: Enable snooping first, verify bindings, trust uplinks, then enable DAI in stages while monitoring inspection counters for false positives.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › DAI Troubleshooting
Stepwise process
  1. Enable DHCP Snooping and confirm bindings for gateways/servers.
  2. Configure uplink interfaces as trusted for both DHCP and ARP inspection.
  3. Enable DAI for a limited VLAN or interface set and monitor counters.
  4. Address missing bindings with static entries or adjust trusted ports.
What to check
show ip arp inspection statistics, show ip dhcp snooping binding, and inspect interface trust state. Correlate drops to missing binding entries.
Example fix
If the default gateway ARP is dropped because its MAC was static, add a static ARP inspection entry or add a matching static binding so DAI accepts the packet.
Common misconception

DAI is not independent — it relies on accurate DHCP bindings. Treat the binding table as the source of truth and correct its gaps before strict enforcement.

screens.title: IP Source Guard (IPSG)
screens.narratorSegment: IP Source Guard prevents IP and MAC address spoofing on untrusted ports by filtering traffic according to the DHCP Snooping binding table. When enabled, the switch checks the source IP and optionally the source MAC of incoming packets on untrusted interfaces. If the packet's source does not match an entry in the binding table, it is dropped. IPSG can operate in IP-only mode or IP-and-MAC mode; IP-and-MAC mode provides stricter enforcement by ensuring both fields match. A practical use case is enabling ip verify source port-security on an access interface where a workstation obtains its address via DHCP: should an attacker configure a static IP that is not in the binding table, IPSG will block that traffic. A common pitfall is enabling IPSG without ensuring the binding table contains static or pre-provisioned entries for devices using fixed addresses; those devices will be blocked. During deployment, prefer IPSG on ports where DHCP is the norm, and confirm bindings first. Consider combining IPSG with Port Security to add a MAC-level restriction in environments that need both IP and MAC controls. What effect would IPSG have on a device manually configured with an IP outside the DHCP pool?

narration.text: IP Source Guard prevents IP and MAC address spoofing on untrusted ports by filtering traffic according to the DHCP Snooping binding table. When enabled, the switch checks the source IP and optionally the source MAC of incoming packets on untrusted interfaces. If the packet's source does not match an entry in the binding table, it is dropped. IPSG can operate in IP-only mode or IP-and-MAC mode; IP-and-MAC mode provides stricter enforcement by ensuring both fields match. A practical use case is enabling ip verify source port-security on an access interface where a workstation obtains its address via DHCP: should an attacker configure a static IP that is not in the binding table, IPSG will block that traffic. A common pitfall is enabling IPSG without ensuring the binding table contains static or pre-provisioned entries for devices using fixed addresses; those devices will be blocked. During deployment, prefer IPSG on ports where DHCP is the norm, and confirm bindings first. Consider combining IPSG with Port Security to add a MAC-level restriction in environments that need both IP and MAC controls. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › IP Source Guard
Definition
Filter traffic using source IP/MAC bindings from DHCP Snooping.
  • Blocks packets whose source IP or IP/MAC pair don't match the binding table.
  • Best for ports where clients receive DHCP-assigned addresses.
  • Can operate in IP-only or IP-and-MAC modes for stricter checks.
Configuration hint
Apply ip verify source port-security on an interface to enable IPSG with port-security integration. Confirm bindings exist before enabling.
Example
On Gi1/0/1, enabling ip verify source port-security will drop traffic if a user manually configures an IP not present in the DHCP binding table. Pair with Port Security for combined MAC/IP enforcement.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a configuration and validation sequence for IP Source Guard on an access port. Begin by ensuring DHCP Snooping is enabled and that the binding table contains the expected lease for the workstation. After applying the configuration, test by attempting to use a static IP not present in the binding table — traffic from that IP should be dropped. screens.title: Storm Control Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Storm Control protects interfaces from excessive broadcast, multicast, or unknown unicast traffic that can consume C P U and bandwidth and cause outages. A storm typically arises from a faulty NIC, misconfiguration, or a Layer 2 loop. Storm Control lets you set thresholds — either as a percentage of link bandwidth or as a packets-per-second value — and when the observed rate exceeds the threshold, the switch drops packets of the specified type until the rate falls below the configured level. A common configuration example is limiting broadcast traffic to 10% on an access link to reduce the risk of a broadcast storm taking down the access segment. When you configure storm-control broadcast level 10.0 on Gi1/0/1, the switch will enforce that threshold. During rollout, monitor counters to ensure you are not trimming legitimate broadcast-heavy applications. A misconception is that a single conservative threshold fits all ports — in practice you should tune thresholds based on expected traffic patterns and consider different settings for uplinks, server ports, and low-activity access ports. How will you determine an appropriate threshold for a mixed-use access port?

keyIdea.title: Storm Control claim
keyIdea.text: Set per-interface thresholds for broadcast, multicast, and unknown unicast to prevent traffic floods from degrading the switch and network.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Storm Control
Definition
Limit traffic rates for broadcast, multicast, unknown unicast.
  • Thresholds can be set as a percentage of bandwidth or packets per second.
  • When exceeded, the switch drops offending traffic until rates normalize.
  • Useful to contain storms from faulty NICs or loops.
Example
On Gi1/0/1 set storm-control broadcast level 10.0 to cap broadcast traffic at 10% of link capacity. Monitor counters for drops during test bursts.
Tuning guidance
Measure normal peak broadcast rates for each port class, then configure thresholds slightly above expected peaks to avoid false positives. Use more aggressive thresholds on edge ports serving unpredictable devices.

screens.title: Errdisable Recovery and Safe Operations
screens.narratorSegment: Errdisable recovery is an operational safety net that can automatically re-enable ports that have been error-disabled due to security violations, such as port-security shutdown. Without errdisable recovery, a shutdown violation leaves the interface down until an operator intervenes, which can cause prolonged outages. To use it, configure errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation and set an interval that balances security and availability, for instance five minutes during testing. When a port moves to errdisabled state, check show interfaces status and show port-security interface to identify the cause. Use errdisable recovery carefully: automatic recovery may hide recurring violations caused by misbehaving devices. A common operational pattern is to start with restrict mode for Port Security and monitor logs; enable errdisable recovery only when you are confident there are no persistent misconfigurations. Another practical step is to combine errdisable recovery with logging and alerting so that re-enabled ports still generate an incident ticket for investigation. When troubleshooting, always examine why the violation occurred before re-enabling the interface to prevent a rapid repeat of the failure. Errdisable Recovery and Safe Operations means use errdisable recovery to reduce user downtime, but pair it with monitoring and investigation to avoid masking persistent problems.. In practical terms, recovering from port shutdowns and minimizing user impact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.5 › Errdisable Recovery
What it does
Automatically recovers error-disabled interfaces after a configured interval. Protects availability but needs monitoring to avoid recurring issues being hidden.
Configuration example
errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation errdisable recovery interval 300 — sets 5 minutes automatic recovery for port-security violations.
Operational note

Always investigate the root cause of an errdisable event; automatic recovery should not replace incident analysis.

Verification
Use show interface status to find error-disabled ports and show port-security interface Gi1/0/1 to see violation counters. Correlate time stamps in logs with recovery intervals.
Example scenario
During initial rollout, set restrict mode and monitor before enabling errdisable recovery. If shutdown is needed, ensure alerts are created when a port is recovered automatically.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential Layer 2 security concepts to keep in mind. Port Security limits MAC addresses and enforces violation actions to prevent MAC table flooding. DHCP Snooping classifies trusted and untrusted ports and builds a binding table used by other features. Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against the DHCP binding table to stop ARP spoofing. IP Source Guard filters traffic by source IP and optionally MAC using the binding table to prevent spoofing. Storm Control sets thresholds to drop excessive broadcast, multicast or unknown unicast traffic to contain storms. Errdisable recovery can automatically re-enable interfaces after security violations but should be used with monitoring to avoid masking persistent faults. These cards summarize dependencies: DHCP Snooping is foundational for DAI and IPSG, and trusted/untrusted classification controls which control-plane messages are allowed on an interface. Keep this dependency map in mind while planning a staged and monitored rollout.

screens.title: What to Remember

fullNarratorScript:
Layer 2 is where most devices first meet the network, and many powerful attacks start there. In this lesson you will learn the essential Layer 2 controls available on Catalyst switches: Port Security to limit MAC learning, DHCP Snooping to prevent rogue servers and starvation, Dynamic ARP Inspection to stop ARP spoofing, IP Source Guard to block IP/MAC spoofing, and Storm Control to contain traffic floods. You will see how these features work together — DHCP Snooping builds a binding table that DAI and IP Source Guard rely on — and where common operational mistakes occur, such as enabling DAI before DHCP Snooping or using shutdown violation actions without errdisable recovery. We will use configuration excerpts and verification commands to show how these controls prevent real attacks like MAC flooding, DHCP starvation, and ARP poisoning. By the end you will understand the practical trade-offs of each feature, a checklist for safe rollout, and a short hands-on scenario to practice configuring and verifying Layer 2 defenses. Think about how access port behavior and trusted/untrusted classification influences the protections you can apply.

In this module you will acquire practical skills to secure the access layer. First, you will identify common Layer 2 attack vectors such as MAC address flooding, DHCP starvation, ARP spoofing, and VLAN hopping. Knowing the attack patterns helps you choose the right control and set thresholds conservatively. Second, you will configure Port Security to limit MAC addresses per port, choose sticky or static bindings, and understand the impact of violation modes. You will practice using protect, restrict, and shutdown and learn when to enable errdisable recovery to minimize outages. Third, you will implement DHCP Snooping — mark trusted and untrusted ports, enable snooping per VLAN, and inspect the binding table to spot anomalies. Fourth, you will enable Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard to validate ARP and IP/MAC bindings based on the DHCP Snooping table, and configure Storm Control to defend against traffic storms. Each objective includes verification steps so you can confirm protections are active and effective in a production-like environment.

Learning to configure controls is only half the task — you must also verify they work and troubleshoot when they don't. In this objective set you'll practice verification commands and interpret their output. For Port Security you will use show commands to list secure MAC addresses, violation counters, and errdisabled state. For DHCP Snooping you'll inspect the binding table to confirm leases and detect suspicious entries. For DAI you'll review arp inspection counters and verify trusted interfaces. For IP Source Guard you'll confirm that source verification is active and that traffic is being filtered for mismatched IP/MAC pairs. Finally, for Storm Control you'll check interface counters and threshold events to confirm the switch is dropping excess broadcast or multicast traffic. Each verification objective includes a common-mistake check: for example, DHCP Offers dropped by an untrusted uplink, or DAI failing because DHCP Snooping was not enabled. These checks help you move from configuration to operational certainty.

Port Security restricts how many MAC addresses a switch port will learn and which MAC addresses are allowed. Its purpose is to reduce the risk from MAC address table flooding attacks and to prevent unauthorized devices from sharing a legitimate endpoint's link. There are three common learning modes: dynamic learning, where the switch learns MACs as devices send traffic; static configuration, where you enter exact MAC addresses you trust; and sticky learning, where the switch learns MACs dynamically but remembers those learned addresses in the running configuration. Violation modes determine the operational response when an unauthorized MAC is seen: protect drops the frames without logging, restrict drops frames and increments a counter and logs events, and shutdown error-disables the interface until manually recovered or errdisable recovery re-enables it. A concrete example is configuring Gi1/0/1 to allow two sticky MACs for a PC and an IP phone. A common mistake is selecting shutdown without errdisable recovery, which can keep a port down for legitimate users after an accidental violation. When you apply Port Security, always monitor violation counters and choose the least disruptive mode that still enforces policy. How would you balance security and availability on a desk with a user and phone?

When a port observes an unauthorized MAC, the switch can respond in three ways: protect, restrict, or shutdown. Protect silently drops frames from unknown MACs and allows normal traffic from known MACs to continue. It is the least disruptive but offers no notifications. Restrict also drops frames, but it increments violation counters and generates logs or SNMP traps, giving visibility while avoiding immediate outage. Shutdown is the strictest: the interface is error-disabled until manually recovered or errdisable recovery re-enables it after a configured interval. This is highly secure because it physically removes the port from forwarding, but it can cause long outages for legitimate users if misapplied. Consider a port that serves both an IP phone and a laptop. If you expect MAC churn, protect or restrict is safer during an initial rollout. If the port is dedicated to a single device in a secure closet, shutdown with errdisable recovery set may be appropriate. Always document expected device counts and test behavior under realistic conditions. A common misconception is that shutdown is always better; in fact, without automated recovery it increases operational risk. Which mode you pick should match your availability requirements, logging needs, and incident response process.

DHCP Snooping defends the network from rogue DHCP servers that can hand out incorrect addresses and from DHCP starvation attacks that exhaust the server's pool. It works by classifying interfaces as trusted or untrusted. Trusted ports are connected to legitimate DHCP servers or upstream switches and are allowed to send all DHCP messages, including server-originated messages like Offer and ACK. Untrusted ports, typically access ports, are restricted and will only forward client-originated messages; server messages from untrusted ports are dropped. DHCP Snooping also builds a binding table mapping client MAC addresses, leased IP addresses, VLANs, and the interface on which the lease was observed. This table becomes a critical source of truth for other features such as Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard. A concrete example is enabling DHCP Snooping globally and for VLAN 10 and marking the uplink port to the distribution switch as trusted. A common misconception is that DHCP Snooping is an isolated feature — in practice it is foundational: enabling DAI or IPSG without a healthy DHCP Snooping binding table will cause false positives. During rollout, monitor the binding table and logs for dropped server messages to ensure trusted uplinks are configured correctly.

The DHCP Snooping binding table is the key artifact produced by DHCP Snooping. It maps client MAC addresses to IP addresses, VLANs, lease times, and the switch interface where the lease was observed. You will use the binding table to identify legitimate leases and spot anomalies such as many leases from the same MAC (possible spoofing) or leases on unexpected interfaces. To verify, run show ip dhcp snooping binding and examine entries for VLAN, MAC, IP, and interface. If you suspect DHCP starvation, watch the binding table for rapid churn or many incomplete bindings. Another verification step is to check which ports are trusted with show ip dhcp snooping interfaces and ensure uplinks to DHCP servers are trusted. Example output shows a binding for 00:11:22:33:44:55 with IP 10.0.10.25 on Gi1/0/1. A common mistake is relying on stale or missing bindings if the snooping database or forwarding path to the database is misconfigured. Always confirm the snooping database is enabled if persistent storage is required, and monitor logs for dropped server messages after toggling trust settings. How would you respond if you saw DHCP Offers dropped from an uplink?

Dynamic ARP Inspection stops ARP spoofing by validating ARP packets against a trusted source of bindings — the DHCP Snooping table. When enabled for a VLAN, DAI inspects ARP requests and replies received on untrusted ports and checks whether the source IP-to-MAC mapping matches an entry in the binding table. If it does not match, the ARP packet is dropped. DAI also validates ARP header fields to prevent malformed ARP frames. Because of this dependency, DHCP Snooping must be enabled and correctly populating bindings before DAI is activated; otherwise legitimate ARP traffic can be mistakenly discarded. A practical example: enable ip arp inspection vlan 10 and mark the uplink as trusted so legitimate ARP replies from the gateway are allowed. A common misconception is that DAI works independently of DHCP Snooping — in reality, absent valid bindings you will see increased drops. When enabling DAI, plan a staged rollout: enable DHCP Snooping, confirm bindings, then enable DAI with monitoring mode or on a small set of interfaces first. This reduces the risk of causing a widespread ARP failure for users.

When enabling Dynamic ARP Inspection, follow a staged process so you avoid unintentionally blocking legitimate traffic. Start by enabling DHCP Snooping and verify the binding table contains expected entries for critical hosts, such as the default gateway and servers. Next, enable DAI on a single VLAN and configure uplink interfaces as trusted. After enabling DAI, monitor show ip arp inspection statistics and show ip dhcp snooping binding to correlate dropped ARP with missing bindings. If you see legitimate ARP being dropped, the likely causes are: DHCP Snooping not enabled on that VLAN, the uplink not configured as trusted, or stale/missing entries in the binding table for statically configured hosts. To handle statically assigned addresses, you can configure static entries in the ARP inspection table or add manual static entries to the binding table where supported. During troubleshooting, consider temporarily placing DAI in a monitoring posture by tracking counters without tight enforcement, or apply DAI to a subset of interfaces first. A misconception is that DAI is an all-or-nothing switch — careful, phased application reduces risk and gives you time to address exceptions.

DHCP Snooping classifies trusted and untrusted ports and builds a binding table used by other features. Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP packets against the DHCP binding table to stop ARP spoofing. IP Source Guard filters traffic by source IP and optionally MAC using the binding table to prevent spoofing. Storm Control sets thresholds to drop excessive broadcast, multicast or unknown unicast traffic to contain storms. Errdisable recovery can automatically re-enable interfaces after security violations but should be used with monitoring to avoid masking persistent faults. These cards summarize dependencies: DHCP Snooping is foundational for DAI and IPSG, and trusted/untrusted classification controls which control-plane messages are allowed on an interface. Keep this dependency map in mind while planning a staged and monitored rollout.

Keep three practical reminders in your pocket. First, DHCP Snooping is foundational: enable and confirm its binding table before enabling DAI or IPSG. Second, choose Port Security modes thoughtfully: start with sticky learning and restrict mode to gather evidence, then tighten to shutdown if operational processes and recovery are in place. Third, tune Storm Control per port class and monitor counters; thresholds that are too low will block legitimate traffic while thresholds that are too high won't protect you. These three practices—establish a trusted binding source, prototype enforcement with visibility, and tune thresholds by measurement—will help you deploy Layer 2 protections safely and effectively. When you face unexpected drops, always check binding tables, trusted/untrusted classification, and violation counters before rolling back protections.
